extracted_by: hand, T-0314 — the Democrat read, May 1834
note: Vol. I No. 23. The advertising page of the town in the first week of May 1834: a small building to let described by its doors and windows, two forwarding houses placed against Fort Dearborn, a tinsmith placed a few doors below one of them, and the port's marine list. The Laughton estate runs through the whole month and starts here.

claims.notes: THE PORT'S OWN COLUMN, and the first of two marine lists this month. It is badly cut — the White Pigeon is entered arriving and clearing on the same date, and the second hull's rig is illegible — so it is claimed for the FACT OF THE TRAFFIC and not for its figures. David Carver, who advertises flour and lumber three columns away, is named here as a consignee, which is the corpus's first sight of a Chicago merchant taking delivery off a named hull. The 28 May list (chicago_democrat_1834_05_28 c001) is legible and carries the month's real count.

claims.notes: A BREAK-IN AT A CHICAGO STORE at the end of April 1834, thirty dollars offered for the detection. The victim's name is lost in the cut and IS NOT SUPPLIED; the 28 May issue carries what is probably the same hand's second notice, at $250 in specie, and the two are NOT merged — the amounts differ and nothing on either line joins them. Kept because a town where a store is worth robbing and a reward is worth printing is a town with goods standing in it overnight.

claims.notes: THE TOWN'S IRONMONGER, AND THE ONLY MAY 1834 TRADE THAT NEEDS A FIRE. Keeney makes tin, sheet iron and copper ware, sells cooking stoves 'with furniture', and — the line that matters for a reconstruction — casts PLOUGHS AND MILL IRONS to order. A shop that furnishes mill castings is a shop with a forge in or behind it, which is a roof feature and a smoke source, not just a frontage. The placement is relative and is the paper's own words: a few doors below Newberry & Dole's, who stand opposite Fort Dearborn (claim c008), so the whole run is anchored to the fort's frontage. The same advertisement stands again on 28 May in a cleaner column.

claims.notes: THE MONTH'S BEST SINGLE BUILDING DESCRIPTION, and it is small. A building that can be either AN OFFICE OR A SMALL FAMILY'S HOUSE is at the bottom of the size range this reconstruction deals — one room or two — and the advertiser thinks its PANEL DOORS and handsome WINDOWS worth the price of type, which in a town of squared logs is a claim to being finished joinery rather than a claim to being large. It stands near Newberry & Dole's, so it is on the fort's side of South Water among the forwarding houses. The advertiser's given name is lost; SWEET is not supplied further.

claims.notes: TWO STRAYED MARES, AND THE GEOGRAPHY IS THE POINT. The notice fixes its ground by 'Laughton's' on the Au Plaine (Des Plaines) river and by a settlement on the DuPage — the same Laughton tavern the estate notices in this issue and through the month are settling, so the family's name is the landmark travellers west of town steer by. The horse descriptions are quoted for their own sake: light chestnut, thirteen or fourteen hands, saddle-gall marks. Working animals at that size are what the town's wagons and hitching posts are scaled to.

claims.notes: BARNARDUS H. LAUGHTON IS DEAD BY 2 MAY 1834, and his widow Sophia takes the administration. This dates a landmark: the Laughton place on the Au Plaine that the estray notice in this same column steers by (claim c006) is, from this month, an estate being wound up, and on 14 May its household goods are sold at the dwelling house itself (chicago_democrat_1834_05_14 c005). Read together the three notices put a named occupied dwelling west of town and then empty it inside four weeks — which is exactly the kind of window ruling 3 asks a survival liberty to cite. A SECOND Laughton estate, David's, is in probate in the adjoining column of the same page, so the two must not be merged: the paper distinguishes them and so does this reading.

business.name: John H. Kinzie

claims.notes: THE FORT IS AN ADDRESS. Kinzie does not name a street; he names the fort and stands opposite it, and so does Newberry & Dole in the very next advertisement (claim c008). That is two of the town's principal forwarding houses placing themselves off Fort Dearborn rather than off the street grid, in May 1834 — which is evidence about what a visitor's eye used as the fixed point, and it is the same phrase both houses are still using in the 1835 issues this corpus already holds. The agency list (Troy N.Y., Galena, Green Bay) is what the frontage was for: this is a lake-and-canal freight house, not a shop. 'Port Dearborn' is the OCR's reading of Fort Dearborn and is left as printed.

claims.notes: THE OTHER FORWARDING HOUSE, and the town's most-cited address in this month's paper: the tinsmith is 'a few doors below' it (claim c003), the building to let is near it (claim c005), and on 28 May a new store opens one door from it on Dearborn street (chicago_democrat_1834_05_28 c004). Newberry & Dole is functioning as the town's coordinate origin in the advertising columns, and its own address is given as the fort — in the 14 May printing of this same advertisement the line 'opposite to Fort Dearborn' sits over it (chicago_democrat_1834_05_14 c007). STORAGE is set first and largest, so the premises are a warehouse before they are anything else.

claims.notes: THE TOWN'S DRUGGIST, and the only May 1834 advertiser who sells a book. Carpenter's stock is the mixed frontier chemist's — drugs, paints, dye-stuffs, oils — with groceries, glass and nails beside them, which is a fair description of what a single shopfront had to carry. The TEMPERANCE ALMANAC FOR 1834 is worth its own line: it is a printed object for sale in Chicago and it dates and names the town's temperance interest. No address is printed in this issue, so the placement is street_only on the town itself.

business.name: J. K. Botsford
business.trade: consignment goods; whiskey, cider, dried apples, glass, groceries; window sash from Detroit

claims.notes: WINDOW SASH KEPT CONSTANTLY, FROM THE FACTORY AT DETROIT — the single most useful line in the month for how the town's buildings were finished. Sash is not being made in Chicago in May 1834; it arrives by lake from Detroit and is held in stock. Glazing is therefore a bought import in standard sizes, and the sizes are printed beside it: 5 by 10 and 7 by 9 glass, twenty boxes and ten. Those are the panes a Chicago window of 1834 is made of, and they bound what any glazed opening in this reconstruction may be. The same column's postscript wants rags, feathers and white mouse skins in exchange for tin ware, which is how far the cash economy did not reach.

business.trade: timber merchant; squared timber and thills

claims.notes: THE TOWN'S TIMBER IS SOLD BY THE STICK AND THE STICKS ARE SIZED. Twelve to sixty feet long, six to fourteen inches square: that is the range of squared structural timber a Chicago builder could buy off the yard in the spring of 1834, and the top of it — sixty feet — is longer than any single member the reconstruction currently builds. It bounds what a warehouse's sills and a wharf's stringers may plausibly be, and it says the material is SQUARE rather than round, which is a silhouette question. Pruyne also advertises a house for sale on the Lasalle and Lake corner three issues later (chicago_democrat_1834_05_21 c001).
